title: Enhanced erosion by continental arc volcanism as a driver of the Cambrian Explosion

paper_content.abstract: Nutrient availability and rising oxygen levels are important for the Cambrian Explosion (~540–515 Ma), both of which can be satisfied via enhanced weathering driven by climate and tectonics. Although increased subduction and continental arc volcanism coincided with the Cambrian Explosion, their weathering-nutrient feedback role remained unclear. Here we integrate Li-Os isotopes with previously published Sr isotope to investigate connections between subduction-driven weathering dynamics and animal diversification. Our results reveal a shift from enhanced erosion of arc-related juvenile rocks (ca. 540–525 Ma) to clay-forming weathering of old crust (525–515 Ma). We propose that subduction-driven warming and uplift may have accelerated erosion of phosphorus-rich juvenile rocks, releasing nutrients that boosted marine productivity and subsequent oxygen buildup through organic burial. This process ultimately fueled early animal diversification, providing additional evidence for tectonic control of biogeochemical cycles during the Cambrian Explosion.
paper_content.introduction:
Continental arcs, where oceanic lithosphere is subducted beneath continental lithosphere, are thought to release more CO2 than other types of volcanoes due to decarbonation of sedimentary carbonates stored in the upper continental plate1,2. As such, the rise and fall of continental arcs pace with Earth’s greenhouse and icehouse intervals since at least the Cryogenian2, strengthening their role in modulating atmospheric CO2 levels and climate change. Elevated arc-related CO2 degassing and associated uplift of continental arcs would then promote silicate weathering and the drawdown of atmospheric CO2, stabilizing the climate system on multimillion-year timescales3–5.

During the Ediacaran–Cambrian transition (E–C), subduction along the Proto-Pacific and Proto-Tethyan margin of Gondwana became active following the final breakup of the Rodinian supercontinent and the initial formation of Gondwana6,7. An increased continental arc length and fraction of young zircon grains indicate enhanced continental arc volcanism during the E–C transition2,8,9, consistent with an increase in atmospheric CO2 and climatic warming2,10. At this time, the rapid rise in animal diversity and abundance (the “Cambrian Explosion”, ca. 540–515 Ma) also occurred11,12. To sustain complex life, nutrient availability (e.g. P, Ca) and oxygen are considered as two important limiting factors13–16, both of which could be affected by enhanced weathering of mountains linked to collision-dominated tectonics during the assembly of Gondwana17,18. However, a large part of the Gondwana assembly-related collisions (mainly before 610 Ma)7 occurred too early to be responsible for the Cambrian Explosion. In contrast, increased subduction-dominated continental arc volcanism along the margin of Gondwana temporally overlapped with the Cambrian Explosion2,8,9. Fast-eroding features of continental arcs, characterized by crustal thickening and intense mantle involvement, may fuel a more efficient feedback loop via CO2 degassing and climatic warming, enhanced weathering of mantle-derived juvenile rocks, and hence the rapid delivery of nutrients to the oceans3,8,19. Along with this feedback process, removal of long-term subduction-related CO2 would result in increased oxygen levels through efficient organic carbon burial that impedes O2 back-reactions10,20. Juvenile rocks from large igneous provinces (LIPs) or arc volcanism typically contain 1.5–2 times higher phosphorus content than continental crust21,22, and are highly susceptible to weathering23. Their rapid weathering would release large amounts of P into ocean, favoring primary productivity, efficient organic burial and O2 production21,22. However, it is not clear whether subduction-driven climatic warming accompanied by enhanced weathering of arc-related juvenile rocks may have played a significant role in the Cambrian biogeochemical cycle and its animal radiation. Additional geochemical evidence is thus required to explore their potential relationship.

Given the fast-eroding features of continental arcs developed upon either a mantle-involved unradiogenic or an ancient continental radiogenic basement, they play an important role in controlling the strontium (Sr) isotopic composition (87Sr/86Sr) of seawater through chemical weathering over geological times4,19. Like Sr, the Os isotope compositions (187Os/188Os) of seawater reflect a balance between two highly distinctive end-member fluxes: unradiogenic sources of 187Os/188Os~0.13 (e.g. extraterrestrial flux, hydrothermal flux and mantle-derived juvenile material weathering) and radiogenic sources of 187Os/188Os~1.4 (e.g. weathering of continental crust)24,25. Thus, variations in seawater 187Os/188Os over geological times can be applied to trace changes in the weathering of juvenile rocks and continental crust24. Besides the Os-Sr isotopes used to trace weathering sources, seawater Li isotope records could provide unique information on silicate weathering rates and regimes in response to climatic changes26,27. δ7Li values of modern rivers vary significantly (3–42‰; average 23‰)27 and depend on the silicate weathering intensity denoted as W/D, which is the ratio of the chemical weathering (W) rate to the total denudation rate (D, consisting of the erosion (E) + chemical weathering (W) rates)27. Low W/D regimes are characterized by high primary rock dissolution, known as congruent weathering with a low dissolved δ7Li and high Li flux, while moderate W/D regimes are linked to secondary mineral (largely clay) formation driving high dissolved δ7Li and a lower Li flux, known as incongruent weathering27,28. In high W/D regimes, there is little rock dissolution and pre-formed secondary clays redissolve, resulting in low dissolved δ7Li and a very low Li flux27,28. The riverine Li makes up over 50% of the modern ocean Li input, with the remainder from mid-ocean ridge hydrothermal inputs and balanced by Li sinks into marine authigenic clays and low-temperature alteration of the oceanic crust28,29. Given the fairly long residence time of Li-Os-Sr isotopes in the modern ocean, they can provide insights into the relationship between weathering dynamics and major paleo-environmental fluctuations25,26,30.

Here, we measured Li isotopes in carbonates and Re-Os isotopes of black shales and cherts that potentially record seawater isotope compositions from two drillcores covering the main interval of the Cambrian Explosion (ca. 560–515 Ma) in the Yangtze Block, South China. With compiled Sr isotope ratios, our work provides critical evidence of subduction-driven weathering dynamics and discusses their role in seawater chemistry and the Cambrian Explosion.
paper_content.results:
The E-C transition witnessed widespread continental arc volcanism along the Proto-Pacific and Proto-Tethyan margin of Gondwana7 (Fig. 1a), such as the Avalonia–Cadomian arcs (750–500 Ma)31, the Ross and Delamerian arcs (590–480 Ma)6,32, and Proto-Tethyan arc (550–490 Ma)33. Some newly generated Large Igneous Provinces (LIPs) were also emplaced around the Central Iapetus on the Laurentian and Baltican cratons (ca. 535–533 Ma)34. The South China, consisting of the Yangtze Block and the Cathaysia Block, was surrounded by an open ocean during the E–C transition period7.

Based on biostratigraphy, radiometric ages (U-Pb and Re-Os), carbon isotope stratigraphy, and marker layers, we have reconstructed a regional stratigraphic framework across the shallow carbonate platform, transitional belt and deepwater slope-basin regions of the Yangtze Block (Fig. 1b, c). The regional black shale (~10 m) of the Doushantuo Member IV is constrained by a U-Pb age of 551.1 ± 0.6 Ma from an ash bed at its top35. Above this layer, the E–C boundary is clearly defined by the globally recognizable basal Cambrian negative carbon isotopic excursions (BACE, N1), and the appearance of small shelly fossils (SSFs) in the shallow shelf Meishucun and Xiaotan sections36 (Fig. 1c). The Liuchapo Formation slope-basin regions traddles the E–C boundary, supported by two U–Pb ages of 542.1 ± 5.0 Ma and 542.6 ± 3.7 Ma from ash beds in the Ganziping and Bahuang sections37 (Fig. 1c), corresponding to the boundary of the Dengying/Yanjiahe Formations in shallow sections. Widespread black shales over the whole Yangtze Block act as a regional marker layer38, constrained by Re-Os ages of 521 ± 5 Ma and 520.3 ± 9.1 Ma for Ni-Mo-V ore layers at the bottom39,40. Thus, the depositional age of the Yanjiahe Formation in the shallow shelf is constrained at ca. 540–521 Ma, time-equivalent to the middle-upper Liuchapo Formation in deep water. Phosphorites are widely distributed in the carbonate platform, with a depositional age of ca. 541–525 Ma based on the U-Pb age of 526.5 ± 1.1 Ma above the phosphorite deposits41,42. Trilobites and more complex, large-bodied animals (e.g., Chengjiang and Qingjiang Biota) also first appeared in the shelf sections at ca. 521–518 Ma38,43 (Fig. 1c).

Core samples covering late Ediacaran to early Cambrian (ca. 560–521 Ma) were collected from carbonates of the Dengying and Yanjiahe Formations in the shallow shelf of drill core ZK4803 (31°28′22“N and 111°11′25“E) and black cherts and shales of the Doushantuo Member IV and Liuchapo Formations in the slope region of drill core ZK4411 (28°02′32“N and 109°04′33“E) (Fig. 2a, b). We measured and calculated Re-Os isochron ages of 557.3 ± 9.1 Ma (2σ, n=9, MSWD=1.6) for the Doushantuo member IV black shales with a high initial 187Os/188Os ratio (Osi) of 0.825 ± 0.086, and 529.1 ± 6.0 Ma (2σ, n=8, MSWD=2.6) for the Liuchapo cherts with evidently low Osi value of 0.341 ± 0.014 (Fig. 2b, c). The continuous Osi records of 560–523 Ma is presented based on their Re-Os data and estimated depositional ages. In general, Osi values stay at a high level with an average of 0.82 at 557 Ma, and 0.62–0.68 at ca. 541–540 Ma, and then rapidly decrease to ~0.34 at ca. 540–525 Ma. After this, they return to high values of 0.76–0.94 at ca. 525–523 Ma (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Data 1). Interestingly, δ7Li values of leached carbonate samples show the same varying trends as Osi, i.e., a general decreasing trend of δ7Li from ~18‰ to ~14‰ at ca. 550–540 Ma, and further to the lowest value of 6.3‰ at ca. 540–525 Ma and then back to a high value of ~17‰ at ca. 525–515 Ma (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Data 2).

Following the typical diagenetic characteristics of modern marine carbonates44,45, additional elemental ratios (e.g., Al/(Mg+Ca), Li/(Mg+Ca) and Sr/(Mg+Ca)) and their relationships with δ7Li are used to evaluate the possible overprint of δ7Li values of ancient carbonates by detrital contamination during carbonate leaching, carbonate mineralogy, and diagenetic alterations. These observations suggest that carbonates in our drill core are most likely formed during marine fluid-buffered diagenesis (Supplementary Figs. S1 and S2), and their δ7Li values are considered to approach the ambient seawater Li isotopic signals with a minor Li isotope fractionation of –0.5‰ to –2‰44,45. More details are given in Supplementary Information.
paper_content.methods:
Sample preparation
Twenty-one fresh core samples of drill core ZK4411 and forty-two carbonate samples of drill core ZK4803 covering 560–515 Ma were selected for Li-Os isotope analysis, and thirty-seven core samples are selected for rare-earth elemental analysis. Core samples were cut into fresh chips and then manually ground to 200 mesh size using an agate mortar and pestle to avoid any metal contaminant. The powered samples were dried and then preserved in a desiccator before instrumental analysis.

Re-Os isotope analysis
The Re-Os chemical separation and analytical methods followed the procedure described by Yin et al. (ref. 59). Approximately 0.2–0.6 g of powdered sample was digested together with 185Re and 190Os enriched spikes in sealed Carius tubes. Prior to sealing, the tubes were frozen in an ethanol–liquid nitrogen freezing bath (–50 to –80°C) and then sealed using an oxygen–propane torch. Digestion was carried out at 220°C for 48 h. Following digestion, osmium was isolated via CCl4 solvent extraction, back-extracted into concentrated HBr, and further purified by microdistillation60. The remaining solution, containing Re, was processed and purified through anion-exchange chromatography. Rhenium concentrations were determined by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS; Thermo Elemental X2 Series). Osmium isotopic measurements were conducted by negative thermal ionization mass spectrometry (N-TIMS) as OsO3⁻ ions loaded onto Pt filaments, using a Thermo-Finnigan Triton instrument operated in electron multiplier mode at the State Key Laboratory of Deep Earth Processes and Resources, Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Reproducibility and accuracy of the Os isotopic measurements were monitored by repeated analysis of the DROsS standard solution, which yielded a mean 187Os/188Os ratio of 0.16094 ± 0.00007 (2σ, n=4), consistent with previously reported values25.

Total procedural blanks (TPBs) averaged 0.41 ± 0.22 pg (2σ; n=4) for Os and 2.9 ± 0.4 pg (2σ; n=4) for Re, with an average 187Os/188Os ratio of 0.286 ± 0.082 (2σ; n=4). All sample data were corrected for the corresponding procedural blank of each analytical batch. The contribution from the blanks was generally negligible. Analysis of the black shale reference material SGR-1b yielded mean values of 187Os/188Os = 1.7857 ± 0.0098, Os = 0.444 ± 0.026 ppb, and Re = 34.67 ± 0.34 ppb (2σ; n=2), which are consistent with certified and literature values59. Regression analyses were performed using IsoplotR61 (https://www.ucl.ac.uk/~ucfbpve/isoplotr/home/). Initial 187Os/188Os values (Osi) were calculated from the measured 187Os/188Os and 187Re/188Os values, and the estimated ages (Supplementary Data 1), with a 187Re decay constant of 1.666 × 10−11/yr62. Total uncertainties include measurement, blank, decay constant, and spike calibration uncertainties, which are reported at the 2σ level.

Li isotope analysis
We targeted the Li isotopic composition of the carbonate core samples. A chemical leaching method using 0.3 M dilute acetic acid was adopted63. After cleaning using deionized water, approximately 200 mg of bulk carbonate sample was leached with 0.3 M acetic acid for at least one hour. After centrifuging, the supernatants were dried and re-dissolved in 1 mL 8 M HCl and dried again. The samples were then dissolved in 2 mL 0.2 M HCl for column purification. Purification of Li for isotope analysis was achieved using an organic solvent-free single-step liquid chromatography procedure in a super-clean lab at Hefei University of Technology. Large columns (4 mL AG 50W-X12 resin, 100–200 mesh) were used to ensure that the column was not saturated for calcium and other cations, which is important for low-Li samples. Separations were monitored with ICP-MS analysis to guarantee both high Li yield [>99.8% recovery] and low Na/Li molar ratio (<0.5)64. The Li yield was calculated using the following equation: Yield (%) = collected Li / (collected Li + pre-yield Li + after-yield Li) × 100%.

The lithium isotopes were measured on a Neptune plus MC-ICP-MS at Hefei University of Technology. The set-up was optimized to achieve both high sensitivity (7Li signal > 6V for 50 ng/g Li solutions, Jet+X cones) and high stability. Solutions for MC-ICP-MS analysis were introduced through a PFA nebulizer (50 μL/min) coupled with a quartz Scott-type spray chamber and were matrix-matched to 10 or 50 ng/g according to the bracketing standards to ensure the best precision and accuracy. The total procedure blanks determined for the combined sample digestion and column procedure were about 0.03–0.14 ng Li. Compared with the ~10–100 ng Li used for our analysis, the blank correction is not significant. Each measurement was bracketed with a L-SVEC standard. The in-run precision of 7Li/6Li measurements is ≤0.2‰ for one block of 30 ratios. The external precision, based on long-term monitoring of two in-house standards, Li = +8.8 ± 0.3‰ (2SD, n>500) and Li = −19.3 ± 0.2‰ (2SD, n>200), is better than 0.5‰. Analysis of international rock reference materials yield δ7Li values of +4.3 ± 0.4‰ (2SD, n=8) for BHVO-2, −0.8 ± 0.2‰ (2SD, n=29) for GSP-2 and +5.9 ± 0.4‰ (2SD, n=9) for AGV-1, which are within the uncertainty of previously published values64.

Rare-earth elemental analysis
Concentrations of rare earth elements were measured by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS, Thermo Scientific Element XR) at the State Key Laboratory of Isotope Geochemistry of Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences. About 40 mg of powdered samples (200 mesh) were digested with a mixture of HNO3 + HCl + HF + HClO4 in high-pressure Teflon cups. The organic-rich samples were firstly combusted in a muffle oven at 650°C for 4 h to completely remove organic matter before dissolution by acids. The analytical standards GSR1 (granite), GSR3 (basalt), SGR-1b (oil shale) plus replicate samples were jointly used to monitor analytical precision, which was better than 7% for rare earth elements.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
I find the manuscript itself is good, and it will benefit from some revisons, but I do not find it suitable for nature. In brief, my main critique is the lack of novelty, and missing literature.
In more detail about my decision:
The authors present this as a novel approach. They present their own Li data, and do a box model calculation with it.
However, if they draw globally valid conclusions, they should use all of the available Li data, or at least explain why they dismiss that. They did use for example Sr global composite, but this is also missing some key data. I am less familiar with Os isotopes, but again a quick search revealed other Os isotope data from that time episode.
The outcome of that study, is that they can show, that only continental arc volcanism could have been the source of volcanism, effectively driving the Cambrian explosion. That is also not very novel, as they themselves state in the introduction, line 61ff. The novelty seems to be the quantification of the activity, which is a good result but not entirely exciting.
Moreover, but not overly relevant, there are some unnecessary self-citations, e.g. line 240 ff.; or 255ff. They use the comparison to other events in different times, merely to state what would have happened if the conditions were different.
I belief the author contributions are missing the info what Sui Ji contributed, and sample collection is mentioned twice in the author contributions.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this revision, the authors clarified the citation for the compiled continental arc length during the E-C transition, and added more reasoning to exclude the contribution from the LIPs to emphasize the arc effect. I am fine with their clarification for the previously miss-cited data compilation, and I do not have much problem with their data and modeling results, but I do think this manuscript would benefit from a more quantitative discussion on their enhanced P flux part.
As reviewer 1 mentioned, continental arc volcanism driving the Cambrian explosion is not really a new idea. The authors’ main contribution in this study is to provide some quantitative constraints on the major contributor to the Li-Sr-Or isotopic system, that there was indeed enhanced arc derived erosion during the E-C transition. Note that this is the only direct conclusion from their data. All the further discussions on how the continental arc activity drive the Cambrian explosion is based on a 240% increase in F_hyd and a 3-4 fold increase of P flux derived through box modeling. My question is whether the increase of continental arc magmatism during the E-C transition could be able to provide such increase in the erosion flux and P flux that match the authors modeling result. Since the authors already have the compiled data of arc duration and length, they should be able to make some estimation of the erosion and elemental flux.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors state the objective of this paper is to explore whether the subduction-driven climatic warming and enhanced weathering of arc-related juvenile rocks played a significant role in the Cambrian Explosion (lines 83-86). From my reading of the ms, the sequence of cause and effect is as follows and differs for the two periods [540-525 Ma] and [525-515 Ma]. Validating the connections in the sequence is important, but I wasn’t fully convinced.
540-525 Ma
1. Tectonic activity: subduction; early stage of continental arc volcanism
2. A: CO2 degassing -> warm climate
B: Uplift of continental arcs -> silicate weathering (drawdown of CO2)
juvenile crust; congruent weathering
3. A: primary productivity; organic matter burial; O2 production
B: Nutrient delivery to the ocean
4. Cambrian Explosion
525-515 Ma
1. Tectonic activity: subduction; later stage of continental arc volcanism
2. A: Decreased CO2 degassing -> warm climate
B: Uplift of continental arcs -> silicate weathering (drawdown of CO2)
old crust; incongruent weathering (clay formation)
3. A: Decreased primary productivity; organic matter burial; O2 production
B: Decreased Nutrient delivery to the ocean
4. Cambrian Explosion slows down?
The difference in the two time periods from my reading of the ms has to do with the stage of continental arc evolution. The first phase (540-525 Ma) involves juvenile crust during initial subduction and the second phase (525-515 Ma) involves older crust. It would help the readers if this distinction was more clearly stated.
To support Step 1, the arc length (Fig. 3F) is given, but the dramatic increase in the arc length predates by ~10 myrs any significant changes in the three isotope systems.
Regarding Step 2A, It would be helpful to have the “sedimentary carbonate stored I the upper continental plate”(line 50) drawn in on Figure 5A and B to show clearly how the release of CO2 is greater for the 540-525 Ma period than the 525-515 Ma period. Is this the platform carbonate on the margin of the continental plate or something interior to the continental crust (grey or green part of Fig 5A and B)? Also, the meaning of different coloring (green and grey) in Fig. 5 is not explained in the caption.
To support increased weathering of juvenile rocks (low Sr and Os isotope ratios 540-525 Ma) and later of older crustal material (high Sr and Os isotope ratios 525-515 Ma), Sr and Os isotope ratio data are used (Fig 3C and E) (Step 2B). Yet, there is a period before 340 Ma where the initial 187Os/188Os and 87Sr/86Sr move in opposite directions. Granted there is a lack Os data points for this period; still, this relationship should be explained. Also, the general statement (lines 87-90) that there is a positive relationship between continental arc length and 87Sr/86Sr does not hold (Fig. 3E and F).
To support congruent weathering of juvenile rocks for the 540-525 Ma period and incongruent weathering and clay formation for the 525-515 Ma period (Step 2B), the authors use lithium isotopes. Over these periods, there has been a shift in carbonate mineralogy from aragonite to calcite. The two mineral types involve different fractionation factors between seawater and carbonate. Shouldn’t this be considered in discussing the d7Li record in Fig 2 and 3D?
The elemental ratios (e.g. Al/(Ca+Mg), Mn/Sr, etc) that are used to test clay contamination or diagenetic alteration for the Li isotope data are a little higher (lenient) than what recent publications use. Also, data points that do not satisfy the cutoff are retained based on the argument that there is no relationship between the isotope ratio and the elemental ratio proxy. This is adopting a rather lenient condition.
To support the increase in nutrients delivered by weathering (Step 3B), the authors give phosphate distribution (Fig. 3B). The data is only qualitative (rare vs. abundant) yet the figure is drawn as if there is a drastic and quantifiable change. This could be misleading. The Ca2+ concentrations changes (Fig. 3B) is based on only two data points and yet the curve is drawn as if there is some structure to it (Fig 3B). I think detailed figure caption or supplementary explanation is necessary.
Authors use multiple isotopes to provide a more robust interpretation (lines 174-176). The lithium and osmium isotope data covering the period of the Cambrian Explosion are new and of interest to the community. The interpretation connecting it to the Cambrian Explosion is interesting and plausible, but the logic needs to be tightened and carefully stated. I realize that the authors may be limited by the length imposed by the journal. Usually, other authors make full use of the Supplement to supply those details.
Minor editorial comments
The material used for isotope ratio measurements should be separately given and the meaning stated briefly (Line 119-123). Are both carbonate and black shales intended to represent seawater values at the time?
In the box model, only a few cases are explored. It would be more persuasive if the authors presented some other combinations of parameter changes (scenarios) they tested in the Supplementary material.
State what the REE pattern for “typical hydrothermal fluids” (line 186) would look like.
State a brief description of the box model used (line 191). For example, it is a dynamic box model.
Consider rewriting lines 194-198, as the meaning does not come through well. The authors are not arguing necessarily for a 50% shorter residence time, per se, but only intend to give this as a extreme scenario. Correct?
Line 61: Add (Fig. 1A).
Line 63: Add (Fig. 3F).
Line 66: Add (Fig. 3A).
Line 69: via -> by
Line 73: mantle-involved -> mantle-derived
Line 302: Cox et al 2016 reference is missing from the list
Fig. 1C: Does [blue star + red age] notation mean something different from [blue star + blue age]?
Fig. 3 Please state in the caption what the pink lines in C, D, E are. Are they rigorously drawn?
F: The numbers given for each of the different arcs don’t match with the ages given in Table S1.

Major concerns 1: Continental arc volcanism as the primary source for the
enhanced juvenile material.
In the manuscript Figure 3, there is a devastating misuse of Cao et al. (2017)’s
continental arc length data (see Figure 1 below). In Cao’s original Figure 4d, continental
arc length decreased after 550 Ma, stayed plateaued, then briefly increased after 500 Ma.
How come in authors’ Figure 3F, they show a sharp increase of continental arc length
right after 550 Ma (which is completely opposite to the trend in Cao’s original graph)?
Interestingly, there appears to be increased total subduction zone length (Mills et al., 2017)
and young zircon proportion (McKenzie et al., 2016) between 560 and 510 Ma. Combined
with the decreasing/steady trend in continental arc length from Cao et al. (2017), it implies
an increase in island arc activities during this period, which, unfortunately, makes the
manuscript’s title and emphasis on continental arcs suspicious (I do not deny on the
2
potential influence from the subduction zone activities, though).
I want to point out that in either Cao et al., 2017, McKenzie et al., 2016, or Mills et
al., 2017 compilation, age constraints are quite loose. For example, McKenzie’s
compilation only has two controlling points for the young zircon proportion between 600
and 500 Ma. Cao’s compilation was based on occurrence of arc-related igneous rocks,
and at least 10–20 Ma uncertainty is expected. Mills’ subduction zone length is largely
based on paleomap plate tectonic reconstructions. None of these original compilations
has the resolution to support for the ~15 Ma decrease in the Os-Sr-Li isotopic values. I
am at odds with the authors stretching data/trends compiled for a much longer time scale
(i.e. the entire Phanerozoic) to “match” their isotopic variations in a small time window,
not mention they did not even copy correctly (similar complaints on their presentation of
the seawater Ca2+ concentration in the manuscript Figure 3B).
In fact, the duration of the observed decrease in the isotopic values (~15 Ma) is a bit
too short for arc erosion. Continental arc erosion usually lasts for ~50 Myr, considering
the deposition duration in back-arc and fore-arc basins. For example, forearc deposition
(with arc igneous rocks as primary source) for the North American Cordilleran arc lasted
from the Late Jurassic to Early Eocene (>40 Ma) (Jiang and Lee, 2017; Kimbrough et al.,
2001; Paterson and Ducea, 2015; Sharman et al., 2015). Similar duration is also
documented in other circum-Pacific and Neo-Tethyan continental arc systems (Wang et
al., 2012). In addition, eroded continental arc materials are in most cases dominated by
andesitic–felsic composition, especially these associated to major magmatic flare-ups
(Dü rr, 1996; Jiang and Lee, 2019; Surpless, 2015), instead of the mafic composition
emphasized by the authors.
The negative Os-Li-Sr isotopic shifts obtained by the authors looks clearly event
3
driven, as the shifts only occur in a 15 Myr time window, prior and after which the isotopic
values shift back to the background. The entire 700–500 Ma period witnessed an overall
enhanced subduction zone activities (including continental arc) (Cao et al., 2017; Mills et
al., 2017). Unless the authors could provide solid evidence that there were intensified arc
magmatic flare-ups right around the 540–525 Ma time window, and the associated

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
I can see that the authors have made a sincere effort to address my previous comments. Most of the other revisions concerning Li isotopes fall outside my area of expertise. However, for the sections that are technically within my domain, I do not have any major remaining concerns, apart from a few comments below, which are intended solely to help the authors avoid potential misunderstandings. At this stage, I believe the manuscript is suitable for publication.
The authors still make special emphasis on eroding of mafic rocks here and there in the manuscript. However, during the majority of continental arc evolution—and particularly during the main phase of intense erosion—the dominant lithologies are typically of andesitic to felsic composition. I already raised this issue in my initial review. While the authors responded using Os-Sr isotopic signatures, they did not consider the lithologic record, which is far more reliable than isotopic evidence alone. I got a feeling that the authors being persistent may be driven by a desire to support the argument for enhanced P and Ca fluxes to the ocean, due to the higher concentrations of these elements in mafic rocks. In arc magmas, there is a strong trend of P saturation towards andesitic composition, and the reason is discussed in Lee and Bachmann (2014). elevated P and Ca fluxes can naturally result from higher denudation rates and runoff, regardless of whether the eroded rocks are mafic. To be clear, I fully agree with the emphasis on "juvenile" or "mantle-derived" rocks. However, I strongly encourage the authors to refrain from repeatedly highlighting “basalt and arc-related mafic rocks” (e.g., lines 84, 281–282), as this is both unnecessary and potentially misleading. Notably, juvenile character and non-mafic arc-related lithology are not mutually exclusive.
Minor issue:
Line 93-94, “Given the fast-eroding features of continental arcs developed upon either an mantle-involved unradiogenic or ancient continental radiogenic basement…” should be “….either a mantle-involved unradiogenic or an ancient continental radiogenic basement…”.
Line 327-329, “It is the enhanced erosion of arc-related juvenile rocks that might have accelerated nutrient availability (e.g., P, Ca) and then raised oxygen levels, promoting Cambrian animal diversity.” Accelerated nutrient availability and raised oxygen levels is not directly related, a link is missing here. Better rephrase this sentence.
Reference
Lee, C.-T. A., and Bachmann, O., 2014, How important is the role of crystal fractionation in making intermediate magmas? Insights from Zr and P systematics: Earth and Planetary Science Letters, v. 393, p. 266-274.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The authors have made substantial improvements in response to earlier reviews. Quantifying phosphorus flux from continental arcs, clarifying the three-stage arc evolution model, and expanding discussion of diagenesis and contamination controls for Li isotopes strengthen the manuscript. The additional calculations linking arc dimensions, erosion rates, and P concentrations to modelled flux increases are a clear step forward.
However, several areas still need clarification and tightening before publication:
1. Geochemical mechanisms
The transition from congruent weathering of juvenile rocks to incongruent weathering of continental crust is central to the argument but not fully explained. The authors should briefly describe why juvenile mafic/intermediate lithologies weather congruently (rapid dissolution, minimal secondary clay retention, low δ⁷Li) and why old felsic crust tends to weather incongruently (feldspar → clay transformation, high δ⁷Li).
The statement that continental arcs can deliver unradiogenic ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr fluxes needs context. Most arcs are radiogenic; unradiogenic flux occurs only when dominated by newly accreted, mantle-derived mafic rocks. This distinction should be made explicit.
2. Terminology and clarity
The phrase “continental clay factory” is used without prior definition; introduce it on first use (e.g., large-scale clay production from incongruent weathering of continental crust).
Replace awkward expressions such as “it is feasibly inferred” with “it is reasonable to infer” or similar.
3. Interpretation issues
Organic-rich shale deposition is typically indicative of low-oxygen marine environments. If the argument is that burial of organic matter led to atmospheric oxygen accumulation, this causal link must be stated explicitly to avoid confusion.
The suggestion that Ca²⁺ flux from juvenile rock erosion “triggered the advent of biocalcification” is speculative, particularly given the sparse seawater Ca²⁺ data. Recast more cautiously as a potential contributing factor coincident with early Cambrian calcifiers.
Evidence for increased continental arc length after 550 Ma should be clearly summarised in the main text, not only shown in Fig. 3F.
4. Figures and data presentation
Phosphate abundance data remain coarse; tonnage estimates help, but measured vs. inferred values should be clearly distinguished in figures.
Sparse Os data before 540 Ma and the limited Ca²⁺ dataset should be flagged prominently in captions to avoid overinterpretation.
Improve figure captions for clarity (e.g., explain colour schemes in Fig. 5; clarify meaning of lines in Fig. 3C–E).
5. Writing quality
Several sentences require tidying for grammar and concision. For example:
“A significant increase of seawater Sr isotope” → “A significant increase in seawater ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr”.
“LIPs only occurred…” → “LIPs during this interval were restricted to the Central Iapetus, covering only ~0.18 × 10⁶ km² and lasting ~2 Myr (535–533 Ma; Fig. 3F; Ernst et al., 2021), making them unlikely to explain a ~15 Myr negative shift in seawater Li–Os–Sr isotopes.”
“It is illustrated that…” → “Both the expansion of active subduction zones along Gondwana’s margin and the increase in continental arc length after ~550 Ma (Fig. 3F) coincide with rising seawater ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr.”
Recommendation
The revision has addressed most substantive concerns and improved the robustness of the conclusions. However, the above clarifications, especially regarding geochemical mechanisms, data limitations, and writing precision, should be addressed before acceptance. I recommend minor revision focused on improving clarity, tightening the prose, and making the causal arguments more explicit.
Anthony Dosseto

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Nutrient availability and rising oxygen levels are important for the Cambrian Explosion (~540–515 Ma), both of which can be satisfied via enhanced weathering driven by climate and tectonics. Although increased subduction and continental arc volcanism coincided with the Cambrian Explosion, their weathering-nutrient feedback role remained unclear. Here we integrate Li-Os isotopes with previously published Sr isotope to investigate connections between subduction-driven weathering dynamics and animal diversification. Our results reveal a shift from enhanced erosion of arc-related juvenile rocks (ca. 540–525 Ma) to clay-forming weathering of old crust (525–515 Ma). We propose that subduction-driven warming and uplift may have accelerated erosion of phosphorus-rich juvenile rocks, releasing nutrients that boosted marine productivity and subsequent oxygen buildup through organic burial. This process ultimately fueled early animal diversification, providing additional evidence for tectonic control of biogeochemical cycles during the Cambrian Explosion.

---

## Introduction

Continental arcs, where oceanic lithosphere is subducted beneath continental lithosphere, are thought to release more CO2 than other types of volcanoes due to decarbonation of sedimentary carbonates stored in the upper continental plate1,2. As such, the rise and fall of continental arcs pace with Earth’s greenhouse and icehouse intervals since at least the Cryogenian2, strengthening their role in modulating atmospheric CO2 levels and climate change. The South China, consisting of the Yangtze Block and the Cathaysia Block, was surrounded by an open ocean during the E–C transition period7.

Based on biostratigraphy, radiometric ages (U-Pb and Re-Os), carbon isotope stratigraphy, and marker layers, we have reconstructed a regional stratigraphic framework across the shallow carbonate platform, transitional belt and deepwater slope-basin regions of the Yangtze Block (Fig. 1b, c). The regional black shale (~10 m) of the Doushantuo Member IV is constrained by a U-Pb age of 551.1 ± 0.6 Ma from an ash bed at its top35. Above this layer, the E–C boundary is clearly defined by the globally recognizable basal Cambrian negative carbon isotopic excursions (BACE, N1), and the appearance of small shelly fossils (SSFs) in the shallow shelf Meishucun and Xiaotan sections36 (Fig. 1c). The Liuchapo Formation slope-basin regions traddles the E–C boundary, supported by two U–Pb ages of 542.1 ± 5.0 Ma and 542.6 ± 3.7 Ma from ash beds in the Ganziping and Bahuang sections37 (Fig. 1c), corresponding to the boundary of the Dengying/Yanjiahe Formations in shallow sections. Widespread black shales over the whole Yangtze Block act as a regional marker layer38, constrained by Re-Os ages of 521 ± 5 Ma and 520.3 ± 9.1 Ma for Ni-Mo-V ore layers at the bottom39,40. Thus, the depositional age of the Yanjiahe Formation in the shallow shelf is constrained at ca. 540–521 Ma, time-equivalent to the middle-upper Liuchapo Formation in deep water. Phosphorites are widely distributed in the carbonate platform, with a depositional age of ca. 541–525 Ma based on the U-Pb age of 526.5 ± 1.1 Ma above the phosphorite deposits41,42. Trilobites and more complex, large-bodied animals (e.g., Chengjiang and Qingjiang Biota) also first appeared in the shelf sections at ca. 521–518 Ma38,43 (Fig. 1c).

Core samples covering late Ediacaran to early Cambrian (ca. 560–521 Ma) were collected from carbonates of the Dengying and Yanjiahe Formations in the shallow shelf of drill core ZK4803 (31°28′22“N and 111°11′25“E) and black cherts and shales of the Doushantuo Member IV and Liuchapo Formations in the slope region of drill core ZK4411 (28°02′32“N and 109°04′33“E) (Fig. 2a, b). We measured and calculated Re-Os isochron ages of 557.3 ± 9.1 Ma (2σ, n=9, MSWD=1.6) for the Doushantuo member IV black shales with a high initial 187Os/188Os ratio (Osi) of 0.825 ± 0.086, and 529.1 ± 6.0 Ma (2σ, n=8, MSWD=2.6) for the Liuchapo cherts with evidently low Osi value of 0.341 ± 0.014 (Fig. 2b, c). The continuous Osi records of 560–523 Ma is presented based on their Re-Os data and estimated depositional ages. In general, Osi values stay at a high level with an average of 0.82 at 557 Ma, and 0.62–0.68 at ca. 541–540 Ma, and then rapidly decrease to ~0.34 at ca. 540–525 Ma. After this, they return to high values of 0.76–0.94 at ca. 525–523 Ma (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Data 1). Interestingly, δ7Li values of leached carbonate samples show the same varying trends as Osi, i.e., a general decreasing trend of δ7Li from ~18‰ to ~14‰ at ca. 550–540 Ma, and further to the lowest value of 6.3‰ at ca. 540–525 Ma and then back to a high value of ~17‰ at ca. 525–515 Ma (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Data 2).

Following the typical diagenetic characteristics of modern marine carbonates44,45, additional elemental ratios (e.g., Al/(Mg+Ca), Li/(Mg+Ca) and Sr/(Mg+Ca)) and their relationships with δ7Li are used to evaluate the possible overprint of δ7Li values of ancient carbonates by detrital contamination during carbonate leaching, carbonate mineralogy, and diagenetic alterations. These observations suggest that carbonates in our drill core are most likely formed during marine fluid-buffered diagenesis (Supplementary Figs. S1 and S2), and their δ7Li values are considered to approach the ambient seawater Li isotopic signals with a minor Li isotope fractionation of –0.5‰ to –2‰44,45. More details are given in Supplementary Information.

## Methods

Sample preparation
Twenty-one fresh core samples of drill core ZK4411 and forty-two carbonate samples of drill core ZK4803 covering 560–515 Ma were selected for Li-Os isotope analysis, and thirty-seven core samples are selected for rare-earth elemental analysis. Core samples were cut into fresh chips and then manually ground to 200 mesh size using an agate mortar and pestle to avoid any metal contaminant. The powered samples were dried and then preserved in a desiccator before instrumental analysis.

Re-Os isotope analysis
The Re-Os chemical separation and analytical methods followed the procedure described by Yin et al. (ref. 59). Approximately 0.2–0.6 g of powdered sample was digested together with 185Re and 190Os enriched spikes in sealed Carius tubes. Prior to sealing, the tubes were frozen in an ethanol–liquid nitrogen freezing bath (–50 to –80°C) and then sealed using an oxygen–propane torch. Digestion was carried out at 220°C for 48 h. Following digestion, osmium was isolated via CCl4 solvent extraction, back-extracted into concentrated HBr, and further purified by microdistillation60. The remaining solution, containing Re, was processed and purified through anion-exchange chromatography. Rhenium concentrations were determined by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS; Thermo Elemental X2 Series). Osmium isotopic measurements were conducted by negative thermal ionization mass spectrometry (N-TIMS) as OsO3⁻ ions loaded onto Pt filaments, using a Thermo-Finnigan Triton instrument operated in electron multiplier mode at the State Key Laboratory of Deep Earth Processes and Resources, Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Reproducibility and accuracy of the Os isotopic measurements were monitored by repeated analysis of the DROsS standard solution, which yielded a mean 187Os/188Os ratio of 0.16094 ± 0.00007 (2σ, n=4), consistent with previously reported values25.

Total procedural blanks (TPBs) averaged 0.41 ± 0.22 pg (2σ; n=4) for Os and 2.9 ± 0.4 pg (2σ; n=4) for Re, with an average 187Os/188Os ratio of 0.286 ± 0.082 (2σ; n=4). All sample data were corrected for the corresponding procedural blank of each analytical batch. The contribution from the blanks was generally negligible. Analysis of the black shale reference material SGR-1b yielded mean values of 187Os/188Os = 1.7857 ± 0.0098, Os = 0.444 ± 0.026 ppb, and Re = 34.67 ± 0.34 ppb (2σ; n=2), which are consistent with certified and literature values59. Regression analyses were performed using IsoplotR61 (https://www.ucl.ac.uk/~ucfbpve/isoplotr/home/). Initial 187Os/188Os values (Osi) were calculated from the measured 187Os/188Os and 187Re/188Os values, and the estimated ages (Supplementary Data 1), with a 187Re decay constant of 1.666 × 10−11/yr62. Total uncertainties include measurement, blank, decay constant, and spike calibration uncertainties, which are reported at the 2σ level.

Li isotope analysis
We targeted the Li isotopic composition of the carbonate core samples. A chemical leaching method using 0.3 M dilute acetic acid was adopted63. After cleaning using deionized water, approximately 200 mg of bulk carbonate sample was leached with 0.3 M acetic acid for at least one hour. After centrifuging, the supernatants were dried and re-dissolved in 1 mL 8 M HCl and dried again. The samples were then dissolved in 2 mL 0.2 M HCl for column purification. Purification of Li for isotope analysis was achieved using an organic solvent-free single-step liquid chromatography procedure in a super-clean lab at Hefei University of Technology. Large columns (4 mL AG 50W-X12 resin, 100–200 mesh) were used to ensure that the column was not saturated for calcium and other cations, which is important for low-Li samples. Separations were monitored with ICP-MS analysis to guarantee both high Li yield [>99.8% recovery] and low Na/Li molar ratio (<0.5)64. The Li yield was calculated using the following equation: Yield (%) = collected Li / (collected Li + pre-yield Li + after-yield Li) × 100%.

The lithium isotopes were measured on a Neptune plus MC-ICP-MS at Hefei University of Technology. The set-up was optimized to achieve both high sensitivity (7Li signal > 6V for 50 ng/g Li solutions, Jet+X cones) and high stability. Solutions for MC-ICP-MS analysis were introduced through a PFA nebulizer (50 μL/min) coupled with a quartz Scott-type spray chamber and were matrix-matched to 10 or 50 ng/g according to the bracketing standards to ensure the best precision and accuracy. The total procedure blanks determined for the combined sample digestion and column procedure were about 0.03–0.14 ng Li. Compared with the ~10–100 ng Li used for our analysis, the blank correction is not significant. Each measurement was bracketed with a L-SVEC standard. The in-run precision of 7Li/6Li measurements is ≤0.2‰ for one block of 30 ratios. The external precision, based on long-term monitoring of two in-house standards, Li = +8.8 ± 0.3‰ (2SD, n>500) and Li = −19.3 ± 0.2‰ (2SD, n>200), is better than 0.5‰. Analysis of international rock reference materials yield δ7Li values of +4.3 ± 0.4‰ (2SD, n=8) for BHVO-2, −0.8 ± 0.2‰ (2SD, n=29) for GSP-2 and +5.9 ± 0.4‰ (2SD, n=9) for AGV-1, which are within the uncertainty of previously published values64.

Rare-earth elemental analysis
Concentrations of rare earth elements were measured by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS, Thermo Scientific Element XR) at the State Key Laboratory of Isotope Geochemistry of Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences. About 40 mg of powdered samples (200 mesh) were digested with a mixture of HNO3 + HCl + HF + HClO4 in high-pressure Teflon cups. The organic-rich samples were firstly combusted in a muffle oven at 650°C for 4 h to completely remove organic matter before dissolution by acids. The analytical standards GSR1 (granite), GSR3 (basalt), SGR-1b (oil shale) plus replicate samples were jointly used to monitor analytical precision, which was better than 7% for rare earth elements.

Major concern 2: Enhanced weathering of juvenile materials drives the

oxygen requirement for large-body, skeletonized animals (Brennan et al., 2004; Wood et
al., 2019; Wei et al., 2024). Although it is not easy to claim that nutrient availability (P,
Ca) and rising oxygen via enhanced weathering of juvenile material are necessary for the
Cambrian explosion, this weathering process at least may have created unprecedented
favorable conditions for the Cambrian Explosion. For example, small shelly fossils were
mainly recorded in phosphorus deposits of South China (Jin et al., 2016). The COPSE

2

atmospheric pO levels to ~0.25 of the present atmospheric level (PAL), which exceeds
2

(Williams et al., 2019). Animal diversification started since Ediacaran (perhaps ~580 Ma)

9
global phosphorus deposits, the Neoproterozoic oxygenation event after GOE, and
climatic warming (Lyons et al., 2014; Reinhard et al., 2017). Enhanced continental arc
volcanism fully match the whole time window of these environmental-biological events,

2024).
Minor concerns

Line 277: “… but is significantly higher than in the preceding period” to “… but is

### Reviewer 2

I can see that the authors have made a sincere effort to address my previous comments. Most of the other revisions concerning Li isotopes fall outside my area of expertise. However, for the sections that are technically within my domain, I do not have any major remaining concerns, apart from a few comments below, which are intended solely to help the authors avoid potential misunderstandings. At this stage, I believe the manuscript is suitable for publication.
The authors still make special emphasis on eroding of mafic rocks here and there in the manuscript. However, during the majority of continental arc evolution—and particularly during the main phase of intense erosion—the dominant lithologies are typically of andesitic to felsic composition. I already raised this issue in my initial review. While the authors responded using Os-Sr isotopic signatures, they did not consider the lithologic record, which is far more reliable than isotopic evidence alone. I got a feeling that the authors being persistent may be driven by a desire to support the argument for enhanced P and Ca fluxes to the ocean, due to the higher concentrations of these elements in mafic rocks. In arc magmas, there is a strong trend of P saturation towards andesitic composition, and the reason is discussed in Lee and Bachmann (2014). elevated P and Ca fluxes can naturally result from higher denudation rates and runoff, regardless of whether the eroded rocks are mafic. To be clear, I fully agree with the emphasis on "juvenile" or "mantle-derived" rocks. However, I strongly encourage the authors to refrain from repeatedly highlighting “basalt and arc-related mafic rocks” (e.g., lines 84, 281–282), as this is both unnecessary and potentially misleading. Notably, juvenile character and non-mafic arc-related lithology are not mutually exclusive.
Minor issue:
Line 93-94, “Given the fast-eroding features of continental arcs developed upon either an mantle-involved unradiogenic or ancient continental radiogenic basement…” should be “….either a mantle-involved unradiogenic or an ancient continental radiogenic basement…”.
Line 327-329, “It is the enhanced erosion of arc-related juvenile rocks that might have accelerated nutrient availability (e.g., P, Ca) and then raised oxygen levels, promoting Cambrian animal diversity.” Accelerated nutrient availability and raised oxygen levels is not directly related, a link is missing here. Better rephrase this sentence.
Reference
Lee, C.-T. A., and Bachmann, O., 2014, How important is the role of crystal fractionation in making intermediate magmas? Insights from Zr and P systematics: Earth and Planetary Science Letters, v. 393, p. 266-274.

### Reviewer 4

The authors have made substantial improvements in response to earlier reviews. Quantifying phosphorus flux from continental arcs, clarifying the three-stage arc evolution model, and expanding discussion of diagenesis and contamination controls for Li isotopes strengthen the manuscript. The additional calculations linking arc dimensions, erosion rates, and P concentrations to modelled flux increases are a clear step forward.
However, several areas still need clarification and tightening before publication:
1. Geochemical mechanisms
The transition from congruent weathering of juvenile rocks to incongruent weathering of continental crust is central to the argument but not fully explained. The authors should briefly describe why juvenile mafic/intermediate lithologies weather congruently (rapid dissolution, minimal secondary clay retention, low δ⁷Li) and why old felsic crust tends to weather incongruently (feldspar → clay transformation, high δ⁷Li).
The statement that continental arcs can deliver unradiogenic ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr fluxes needs context. Most arcs are radiogenic; unradiogenic flux occurs only when dominated by newly accreted, mantle-derived mafic rocks. This distinction should be made explicit.
2. Terminology and clarity
The phrase “continental clay factory” is used without prior definition; introduce it on first use (e.g., large-scale clay production from incongruent weathering of continental crust).
Replace awkward expressions such as “it is feasibly inferred” with “it is reasonable to infer” or similar.
3. Interpretation issues
Organic-rich shale deposition is typically indicative of low-oxygen marine environments. If the argument is that burial of organic matter led to atmospheric oxygen accumulation, this causal link must be stated explicitly to avoid confusion.
The suggestion that Ca²⁺ flux from juvenile rock erosion “triggered the advent of biocalcification” is speculative, particularly given the sparse seawater Ca²⁺ data. Recast more cautiously as a potential contributing factor coincident with early Cambrian calcifiers.
Evidence for increased continental arc length after 550 Ma should be clearly summarised in the main text, not only shown in Fig. 3F.
4. Figures and data presentation
Phosphate abundance data remain coarse; tonnage estimates help, but measured vs. inferred values should be clearly distinguished in figures.
Sparse Os data before 540 Ma and the limited Ca²⁺ dataset should be flagged prominently in captions to avoid overinterpretation.
Improve figure captions for clarity (e.g., explain colour schemes in Fig. 5; clarify meaning of lines in Fig. 3C–E).
5. Writing quality
Several sentences require tidying for grammar and concision. For example:
“A significant increase of seawater Sr isotope” → “A significant increase in seawater ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr”.
“LIPs only occurred…” → “LIPs during this interval were restricted to the Central Iapetus, covering only ~0.18 × 10⁶ km² and lasting ~2 Myr (535–533 Ma; Fig. 3F; Ernst et al., 2021), making them unlikely to explain a ~15 Myr negative shift in seawater Li–Os–Sr isotopes.”
“It is illustrated that…” → “Both the expansion of active subduction zones along Gondwana’s margin and the increase in continental arc length after ~550 Ma (Fig. 3F) coincide with rising seawater ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr.”
Recommendation
The revision has addressed most substantive concerns and improved the robustness of the conclusions. However, the above clarifications, especially regarding geochemical mechanisms, data limitations, and writing precision, should be addressed before acceptance. I recommend minor revision focused on improving clarity, tightening the prose, and making the causal arguments more explicit.
Anthony Dosseto

## Paper

## Abstract

Nutrient availability and rising oxygen levels are important for the Cambrian Explosion (~540–515 Ma), both of which can be satisfied via enhanced weathering driven by climate and tectonics. Although increased subduction and continental arc volcanism coincided with the Cambrian Explosion, their weathering-nutrient feedback role remained unclear. Here we integrate Li-Os isotopes with previously published Sr isotope to investigate connections between subduction-driven weathering dynamics and animal diversification. Our results reveal a shift from enhanced erosion of arc-related juvenile rocks (ca. 540–525 Ma) to clay-forming weathering of old crust (525–515 Ma). We propose that subduction-driven warming and uplift may have accelerated erosion of phosphorus-rich juvenile rocks, releasing nutrients that boosted marine productivity and subsequent oxygen buildup through organic burial. This process ultimately fueled early animal diversification, providing additional evidence for tectonic control of biogeochemical cycles during the Cambrian Explosion.

---

## Introduction

Continental arcs, where oceanic lithosphere is subducted beneath continental lithosphere, are thought to release more CO2 than other types of volcanoes due to decarbonation of sedimentary carbonates stored in the upper continental plate1,2. As such, the rise and fall of continental arcs pace with Earth’s greenhouse and icehouse intervals since at least the Cryogenian2, strengthening their role in modulating atmospheric CO2 levels and climate change. Elevated arc-related CO2 degassing and associated uplift of continental arcs would then promote silicate weathering and the drawdown of atmospheric CO2, stabilizing the climate system on multimillion-year timescales3–5.

During the Ediacaran–Cambrian transition (E–C), subduction along the Proto-Pacific and Proto-Tethyan margin of Gondwana became active following the final breakup of the Rodinian supercontinent and the initial formation of Gondwana6,7. An increased continental arc length and fraction of young zircon grains indicate enhanced continental arc volcanism during the E–C transition2,8,9, consistent with an increase in atmospheric CO2 and climatic warming2,10. At this time, the rapid rise in animal diversity and abundance (the “Cambrian Explosion”, ca. 540–515 Ma) also occurred11,12. To sustain complex life, nutrient availability (e.g. P, Ca) and oxygen are considered as two important limiting factors13–16, both of which could be affected by enhanced weathering of mountains linked to collision-dominated tectonics during the assembly of Gondwana17,18. However, a large part of the Gondwana assembly-related collisions (mainly before 610 Ma)7 occurred too early to be responsible for the Cambrian Explosion. In contrast, increased subduction-dominated continental arc volcanism along the margin of Gondwana temporally overlapped with the Cambrian Explosion2,8,9. Fast-eroding features of continental arcs, characterized by crustal thickening and intense mantle involvement, may fuel a more efficient feedback loop via CO2 degassing and climatic warming, enhanced weathering of mantle-derived juvenile rocks, and hence the rapid delivery of nutrients to the oceans3,8,19. Along with this feedback process, removal of long-term subduction-related CO2 would result in increased oxygen levels through efficient organic carbon burial that impedes O2 back-reactions10,20. Juvenile rocks from large igneous provinces (LIPs) or arc volcanism typically contain 1.5–2 times higher phosphorus content than continental crust21,22, and are highly susceptible to weathering23. Their rapid weathering would release large amounts of P into ocean, favoring primary productivity, efficient organic burial and O2 production21,22. However, it is not clear whether subduction-driven climatic warming accompanied by enhanced weathering of arc-related juvenile rocks may have played a significant role in the Cambrian biogeochemical cycle and its animal radiation. Additional geochemical evidence is thus required to explore their potential relationship.

Given the fast-eroding features of continental arcs developed upon either a mantle-involved unradiogenic or an ancient continental radiogenic basement, they play an important role in controlling the strontium (Sr) isotopic composition (87Sr/86Sr) of seawater through chemical weathering over geological times4,19. Like Sr, the Os isotope compositions (187Os/188Os) of seawater reflect a balance between two highly distinctive end-member fluxes: unradiogenic sources of 187Os/188Os~0.13 (e.g. extraterrestrial flux, hydrothermal flux and mantle-derived juvenile material weathering) and radiogenic sources of 187Os/188Os~1.4 (e.g. weathering of continental crust)24,25. Thus, variations in seawater 187Os/188Os over geological times can be applied to trace changes in the weathering of juvenile rocks and continental crust24. Besides the Os-Sr isotopes used to trace weathering sources, seawater Li isotope records could provide unique information on silicate weathering rates and regimes in response to climatic changes26,27. δ7Li values of modern rivers vary significantly (3–42‰; average 23‰)27 and depend on the silicate weathering intensity denoted as W/D, which is the ratio of the chemical weathering (W) rate to the total denudation rate (D, consisting of the erosion (E) + chemical weathering (W) rates)27. Low W/D regimes are characterized by high primary rock dissolution, known as congruent weathering with a low dissolved δ7Li and high Li flux, while moderate W/D regimes are linked to secondary mineral (largely clay) formation driving high dissolved δ7Li and a lower Li flux, known as incongruent weathering27,28. In high W/D regimes, there is little rock dissolution and pre-formed secondary clays redissolve, resulting in low dissolved δ7Li and a very low Li flux27,28. The riverine Li makes up over 50% of the modern ocean Li input, with the remainder from mid-ocean ridge hydrothermal inputs and balanced by Li sinks into marine authigenic clays and low-temperature alteration of the oceanic crust28,29. Given the fairly long residence time of Li-Os-Sr isotopes in the modern ocean, they can provide insights into the relationship between weathering dynamics and major paleo-environmental fluctuations25,26,30.

Here, we measured Li isotopes in carbonates and Re-Os isotopes of black shales and cherts that potentially record seawater isotope compositions from two drillcores covering the main interval of the Cambrian Explosion (ca. 560–515 Ma) in the Yangtze Block, South China. With compiled Sr isotope ratios, our work provides critical evidence of subduction-driven weathering dynamics and discusses their role in seawater chemistry and the Cambrian Explosion.

---

## Results

The E-C transition witnessed widespread continental arc volcanism along the Proto-Pacific and Proto-Tethyan margin of Gondwana7 (Fig. 1a), such as the Avalonia–Cadomian arcs (750–500 Ma)31, the Ross and Delamerian arcs (590–480 Ma)6,32, and Proto-Tethyan arc (550–490 Ma)33. Some newly generated Large Igneous Provinces (LIPs) were also emplaced around the Central Iapetus on the Laurentian and Baltican cratons (ca. 535–533 Ma)34. The South China, consisting of the Yangtze Block and the Cathaysia Block, was surrounded by an open ocean during the E–C transition period7.

Based on biostratigraphy, radiometric ages (U-Pb and Re-Os), carbon isotope stratigraphy, and marker layers, we have reconstructed a regional stratigraphic framework across the shallow carbonate platform, transitional belt and deepwater slope-basin regions of the Yangtze Block (Fig. 1b, c). The regional black shale (~10 m) of the Doushantuo Member IV is constrained by a U-Pb age of 551.1 ± 0.6 Ma from an ash bed at its top35. Above this layer, the E–C boundary is clearly defined by the globally recognizable basal Cambrian negative carbon isotopic excursions (BACE, N1), and the appearance of small shelly fossils (SSFs) in the shallow shelf Meishucun and Xiaotan sections36 (Fig. 1c). The Liuchapo Formation slope-basin regions traddles the E–C boundary, supported by two U–Pb ages of 542.1 ± 5.0 Ma and 542.6 ± 3.7 Ma from ash beds in the Ganziping and Bahuang sections37 (Fig. 1c), corresponding to the boundary of the Dengying/Yanjiahe Formations in shallow sections. Widespread black shales over the whole Yangtze Block act as a regional marker layer38, constrained by Re-Os ages of 521 ± 5 Ma and 520.3 ± 9.1 Ma for Ni-Mo-V ore layers at the bottom39,40. Thus, the depositional age of the Yanjiahe Formation in the shallow shelf is constrained at ca. 540–521 Ma, time-equivalent to the middle-upper Liuchapo Formation in deep water. Phosphorites are widely distributed in the carbonate platform, with a depositional age of ca. 541–525 Ma based on the U-Pb age of 526.5 ± 1.1 Ma above the phosphorite deposits41,42. Trilobites and more complex, large-bodied animals (e.g., Chengjiang and Qingjiang Biota) also first appeared in the shelf sections at ca. 521–518 Ma38,43 (Fig. 1c).

Core samples covering late Ediacaran to early Cambrian (ca. 560–521 Ma) were collected from carbonates of the Dengying and Yanjiahe Formations in the shallow shelf of drill core ZK4803 (31°28′22“N and 111°11′25“E) and black cherts and shales of the Doushantuo Member IV and Liuchapo Formations in the slope region of drill core ZK4411 (28°02′32“N and 109°04′33“E) (Fig. 2a, b). We measured and calculated Re-Os isochron ages of 557.3 ± 9.1 Ma (2σ, n=9, MSWD=1.6) for the Doushantuo member IV black shales with a high initial 187Os/188Os ratio (Osi) of 0.825 ± 0.086, and 529.1 ± 6.0 Ma (2σ, n=8, MSWD=2.6) for the Liuchapo cherts with evidently low Osi value of 0.341 ± 0.014 (Fig. 2b, c). The continuous Osi records of 560–523 Ma is presented based on their Re-Os data and estimated depositional ages. In general, Osi values stay at a high level with an average of 0.82 at 557 Ma, and 0.62–0.68 at ca. 541–540 Ma, and then rapidly decrease to ~0.34 at ca. 540–525 Ma. After this, they return to high values of 0.76–0.94 at ca. 525–523 Ma (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Data 1). Interestingly, δ7Li values of leached carbonate samples show the same varying trends as Osi, i.e., a general decreasing trend of δ7Li from ~18‰ to ~14‰ at ca. 550–540 Ma, and further to the lowest value of 6.3‰ at ca. 540–525 Ma and then back to a high value of ~17‰ at ca. 525–515 Ma (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Data 2).

Following the typical diagenetic characteristics of modern marine carbonates44,45, additional elemental ratios (e.g., Al/(Mg+Ca), Li/(Mg+Ca) and Sr/(Mg+Ca)) and their relationships with δ7Li are used to evaluate the possible overprint of δ7Li values of ancient carbonates by detrital contamination during carbonate leaching, carbonate mineralogy, and diagenetic alterations. These observations suggest that carbonates in our drill core are most likely formed during marine fluid-buffered diagenesis (Supplementary Figs. S1 and S2), and their δ7Li values are considered to approach the ambient seawater Li isotopic signals with a minor Li isotope fractionation of –0.5‰ to –2‰44,45. More details are given in Supplementary Information.

---

## Methods

Sample preparation
Twenty-one fresh core samples of drill core ZK4411 and forty-two carbonate samples of drill core ZK4803 covering 560–515 Ma were selected for Li-Os isotope analysis, and thirty-seven core samples are selected for rare-earth elemental analysis. Core samples were cut into fresh chips and then manually ground to 200 mesh size using an agate mortar and pestle to avoid any metal contaminant. The powered samples were dried and then preserved in a desiccator before instrumental analysis.

Re-Os isotope analysis
The Re-Os chemical separation and analytical methods followed the procedure described by Yin et al. (ref. 59). Approximately 0.2–0.6 g of powdered sample was digested together with 185Re and 190Os enriched spikes in sealed Carius tubes. Prior to sealing, the tubes were frozen in an ethanol–liquid nitrogen freezing bath (–50 to –80°C) and then sealed using an oxygen–propane torch. Digestion was carried out at 220°C for 48 h. Following digestion, osmium was isolated via CCl4 solvent extraction, back-extracted into concentrated HBr, and further purified by microdistillation60. The remaining solution, containing Re, was processed and purified through anion-exchange chromatography. Rhenium concentrations were determined by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS; Thermo Elemental X2 Series). Osmium isotopic measurements were conducted by negative thermal ionization mass spectrometry (N-TIMS) as OsO3⁻ ions loaded onto Pt filaments, using a Thermo-Finnigan Triton instrument operated in electron multiplier mode at the State Key Laboratory of Deep Earth Processes and Resources, Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Reproducibility and accuracy of the Os isotopic measurements were monitored by repeated analysis of the DROsS standard solution, which yielded a mean 187Os/188Os ratio of 0.16094 ± 0.00007 (2σ, n=4), consistent with previously reported values25.

Total procedural blanks (TPBs) averaged 0.41 ± 0.22 pg (2σ; n=4) for Os and 2.9 ± 0.4 pg (2σ; n=4) for Re, with an average 187Os/188Os ratio of 0.286 ± 0.082 (2σ; n=4). All sample data were corrected for the corresponding procedural blank of each analytical batch. The contribution from the blanks was generally negligible. Analysis of the black shale reference material SGR-1b yielded mean values of 187Os/188Os = 1.7857 ± 0.0098, Os = 0.444 ± 0.026 ppb, and Re = 34.67 ± 0.34 ppb (2σ; n=2), which are consistent with certified and literature values59. Regression analyses were performed using IsoplotR61 (https://www.ucl.ac.uk/~ucfbpve/isoplotr/home/). Initial 187Os/188Os values (Osi) were calculated from the measured 187Os/188Os and 187Re/188Os values, and the estimated ages (Supplementary Data 1), with a 187Re decay constant of 1.666 × 10−11/yr62. Total uncertainties include measurement, blank, decay constant, and spike calibration uncertainties, which are reported at the 2σ level.

Li isotope analysis
We targeted the Li isotopic composition of the carbonate core samples. A chemical leaching method using 0.3 M dilute acetic acid was adopted63. After cleaning using deionized water, approximately 200 mg of bulk carbonate sample was leached with 0.3 M acetic acid for at least one hour. After centrifuging, the supernatants were dried and re-dissolved in 1 mL 8 M HCl and dried again. The samples were then dissolved in 2 mL 0.2 M HCl for column purification. Purification of Li for isotope analysis was achieved using an organic solvent-free single-step liquid chromatography procedure in a super-clean lab at Hefei University of Technology. Large columns (4 mL AG 50W-X12 resin, 100–200 mesh) were used to ensure that the column was not saturated for calcium and other cations, which is important for low-Li samples. Separations were monitored with ICP-MS analysis to guarantee both high Li yield [>99.8% recovery] and low Na/Li molar ratio (<0.5)64. The Li yield was calculated using the following equation: Yield (%) = collected Li / (collected Li + pre-yield Li + after-yield Li) × 100%.

The lithium isotopes were measured on a Neptune plus MC-ICP-MS at Hefei University of Technology. The set-up was optimized to achieve both high sensitivity (7Li signal > 6V for 50 ng/g Li solutions, Jet+X cones) and high stability. Solutions for MC-ICP-MS analysis were introduced through a PFA nebulizer (50 μL/min) coupled with a quartz Scott-type spray chamber and were matrix-matched to 10 or 50 ng/g according to the bracketing standards to ensure the best precision and accuracy. The total procedure blanks determined for the combined sample digestion and column procedure were about 0.03–0.14 ng Li. Compared with the ~10–100 ng Li used for our analysis, the blank correction is not significant. Each measurement was bracketed with a L-SVEC standard. The in-run precision of 7Li/6Li measurements is ≤0.2‰ for one block of 30 ratios. The external precision, based on long-term monitoring of two in-house standards, Li = +8.8 ± 0.3‰ (2SD, n>500) and Li = −19.3 ± 0.2‰ (2SD, n>200), is better than 0.5‰. Analysis of international rock reference materials yield δ7Li values of +4.3 ± 0.4‰ (2SD, n=8) for BHVO-2, −0.8 ± 0.2‰ (2SD, n=29) for GSP-2 and +5.9 ± 0.4‰ (2SD, n=9) for AGV-1, which are within the uncertainty of previously published values64.

Rare-earth elemental analysis
Concentrations of rare earth elements were measured by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS, Thermo Scientific Element XR) at the State Key Laboratory of Isotope Geochemistry of Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences. About 40 mg of powdered samples (200 mesh) were digested with a mixture of HNO3 + HCl + HF + HClO4 in high-pressure Teflon cups. The organic-rich samples were firstly combusted in a muffle oven at 650°C for 4 h to completely remove organic matter before dissolution by acids. The analytical standards GSR1 (granite), GSR3 (basalt), SGR-1b (oil shale) plus replicate samples were jointly used to monitor analytical precision, which was better than 7% for rare earth elements.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

I find the manuscript itself is good, and it will benefit from some revisons, but I do not find it suitable for nature. In brief, my main critique is the lack of novelty, and missing literature.
In more detail about my decision:
The authors present this as a novel approach. They present their own Li data, and do a box model calculation with it.
However, if they draw globally valid conclusions, they should use all of the available Li data, or at least explain why they dismiss that. They did use for example Sr global composite, but this is also missing some key data. I am less familiar with Os isotopes, but again a quick search revealed other Os isotope data from that time episode.
The outcome of that study, is that they can show, that only continental arc volcanism could have been the source of volcanism, effectively driving the Cambrian explosion. That is also not very novel, as they themselves state in the introduction, line 61ff. The novelty seems to be the quantification of the activity, which is a good result but not entirely exciting.
Moreover, but not overly relevant, there are some unnecessary self-citations, e.g. line 240 ff.; or 255ff. They use the comparison to other events in different times, merely to state what would have happened if the conditions were different.
I belief the author contributions are missing the info what Sui Ji contributed, and sample collection is mentioned twice in the author contributions.

### Reviewer 2

In this revision, the authors clarified the citation for the compiled continental arc length during the E-C transition, and added more reasoning to exclude the contribution from the LIPs to emphasize the arc effect. I am fine with their clarification for the previously miss-cited data compilation, and I do not have much problem with their data and modeling results, but I do think this manuscript would benefit from a more quantitative discussion on their enhanced P flux part.
As reviewer 1 mentioned, continental arc volcanism driving the Cambrian explosion is not really a new idea.
